questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Honestly I just wanted a break from my everyday life, get far way, and experience something completely new. I chose Japan more specifically because it seemed like a country, that was in the easier end to navigate even when you hadn't been there before, spoke the language or knew a lot about it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Some was easy, some was hard. It takes some energy getting used to a country, where you can't read anything or don't know where to go for anything. I especially found it hard to navigate some of the more formal aspects of moving in like registering at the city office and things like that. But asking housemates and people at uni will get you far.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They had an offer about course registration at the university, that was really helpful. But generally I think Waseda is good at providing information about everything related to the University. They also send you a comprehensive guide on what you need to do upon arrival in Japan. Other than that I just asked people around me, when I was confused;)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I applied for the university dorms, but I didn't get a spot. But Waseda also has a separate page with links to other places you can find housing. I found housing through a sharehouse company called Oakhouse. They have a lot of sharehouses around the country, and it was really easy to navigate their site, and I enjoyed it. I know other students found housing through a similar company called BeGood Japan and liked that as well.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I was really glad, that I chose a shared housing option, since Waseda does not have many social events, and I really appreciated hanging out with my housemates as well. In the dorms everyone is studying and from what I've heard most people are around 18 to start 20s. At off-campus living options that obviously differs. From what I've heard, there is a lot of internationals in most sharehouses, but it is very different how old they are, and what they are doing (studying, working etc.). But in my experience, it is still very likely, that you will meet people. And I also enjoyed getting to know people who did different things in the city than studying too.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived in Koenji and I can really recommend that (and also Kichijoji), if you want to live in an area, that is a little less busy than e.g. Shinjuku, but still close to Waseda. I also got a bike, which I can also only recommend.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You register for courses online, and have the opportunity to drop or change courses in the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They offered a course registration guide meeting, which was really helpful

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successful. There were a couple courses i didn't get, and some of the ones I wanted were at the same time, but I got most of what I wanted, and I think most students did.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Ask your home university if you are able to change your preapproved courses before you leave, so you know, if you can change to other courses at Waseda, if you find something else that you want. It is really easy to change courses at Waseda in the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Compared to UCPH I found the academic level of the courses much lower. But I also mostly took introductory courses, so that could also be why.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A lot of the courses I had at Waseda was based on student discussion. It was really giving and interesting to hear everyone's perspectives and thoughts since the student group was quite diverse. But I missed classic lectures and exercises, and didn't feel like the teaching was as focused on tools and theories as it is at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Monozukuri Culture in Japanese Society, Problem / Conflict Analysis and Resolution, Global Food Security: Demand and Supply Challenges, Topics in Social and Economic Development 1, Contemporary Japanese Foreign Policy, The Inside of Peacebuilding, Topics in Sustainable Development, Diversity in Modern Japan 2

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can really recommend Monozukuri Culture in Japanese Society! It was an easy but very interesting course about Japanese making-culture, and the professor was super sweet. 

I also recommend taking one of -NAME REDACTED- 's courses (I had Topics in Social and Economic Development 1 and Topics in Sustainable Development). They are discussion based and quite nice. But I would also only recommend taking 1 of his courses since the workload is heavy compared to other courses and they are really similar (both in style and topics), so you don't really learn much more from taking two.

Housing DKK per month *

Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I just spend a lot more money than expected on snacks and drinks at the konbini. Because it was so cheap, I bought it all the time haha.
Also we had cockroaches and mice at the house, so I didn't cook much - I mostly ate out.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation is quite expensive. Food and snacks is very cheap though.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were some, but it didn't seem super accessible to exchange students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You could go to some events, but it was mostly just a quiz and a speed-date-topic-talk and a glass of coca cola.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the sento every time you are tired or hungover!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend going hiking, but a lot of hikes a pretty unaccessible in the winter, so do some research if you are into it. Also go to kamakura and enoshima on a weekend, it is really beautiful and nice.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It took a while. But also because I couldn't speak or read any Japanese upon arrival.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Ask people to go for lunch. Or invite people you meet along, if there is something you want to go see or do.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I think I found it the most challenging, that the gender norms are quite different from Denmark. Also I sometimes found it hard sometimes to stick out so much by looks (taller, blonde, etc.), since there is very much a culture of not taking up space in public spaces, and it is easy to feel like you are out of place or taking up too much space by just being.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: On the other hand I also really like the culture of respecting the public space. And of course everyone is really friendly and polite. I also really appreciated getting a look into the way nature, space, aesthetics, and religion play a big role in the culture and cityspace.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Enjoy it all you can. Go see some of the breathtaking nature. And take use of the fact that you can finally eat out without breaking the bank.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The application process at Waseda is quite tedious, but it is very worth it at the end. 
Also the credits of the courses do not count for much in the UCPH transfer, so you have to take a lot of courses, but don't worry. The courseload in total is not much heavier, and it is very much doable while still having free time.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting sweet people, that I will have in my life forever.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Trying to go to the gynecologist that you can't really speak to:)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
